summary: Defines how to run IP and ARP over an ATM network set up as a logical IP subnet. IP addresses are mapped to ATM addresses through a server. It replaces RFC 1577 and RFC 1626.

eli5.summary: It explains how the Internet's address system can run on a different kind of network by keeping a directory that turns one kind of address into the other.

what is a logical ip subnet in atm
what is a logical ip subnet
what is the default mtu for ip over atm
subtitle: How IP datagrams and address lookups run over an ATM network treated like an ordinary LAN subnet.

tldr.problem: ATM networks work with virtual connections and ATM addresses, but IP hosts need to find each other by IP address and send datagrams as if on a normal LAN segment.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts form a Logical IP Subnetwork, send IP in LLC/SNAP-encapsulated AAL5 frames with a default MTU of 9180 octets, and resolve IP addresses to ATM addresses by asking a single ATMARP server.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 1577 and RFC 1626 and is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 5494. It leaves broadcast and multicast mappings to future work.

today: RFC 2225 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 1577 and RFC 1626, and it has been updated by RFC 5494.

sections.title: The Classical Model
sections.content:
RFC 2225 defines how to send IP datagrams and ATMARP requests and replies over ATM Adaptation Layer 5 (AAL5). It treats ATM as a direct replacement for the wires and LAN segments that join IP hosts and routers, which the RFC calls the classical model. The ATM host adapter is just another network interface for the IP stack.

The RFC says it describes only a stable baseline that will always be available. Later memos may build on it, but without them operation defaults to this document. ATM networks that are globally connected, MAC-level bridging and LAN emulation are out of scope.

Some ATM background is given. Data on a virtual connection is cut into 53 octet cells, 5 octets of header and 48 of data. AAL5 carries packets of up to (64K - 1) octets, keeps cell order on a given connection, and gives a non-assured service, so higher protocols must handle retransmission. Connections can be permanent (PVC) or switched (SVC), and ATM addresses are either ATM Forum NSAP-style addresses or E.164 numbers.
sections.eli5: ATM is a different kind of road system. This document says how to drive the usual Internet cars on those roads as if nothing had changed.

sections.title: The Logical IP Subnetwork
sections.content:
Each administrative entity sets up its hosts and routers as a Logical IP Subnetwork (LIS). Each LIS works independently of other LISs on the same ATM network. Hosts talk directly over ATM to other hosts in the same LIS, and reach hosts outside it through an IP router. Hosts on different IP subnets MUST go through a router, even if a direct virtual connection would be possible.

All members of a LIS share the same IP network or subnet number and address mask, are directly attached to the ATM network, and can reach every other member, so the virtual connections form a full mesh. Every member MUST be able to resolve IP to ATM addresses with ATMARP and the reverse with InATMARP when using SVCs, and to resolve virtual connections to IP addresses with InATMARP when using PVCs.

Each station MUST hold its own ATM address (atm$ha) and a list of ATMARP server addresses (atm$arp-req-list). A LIS MUST have a single ATMARP service available to all SVC users. A PVC-only member has an all-null list and must not query a resolution service. By default the list is configured using the MIB, and the RFC does not require any particular configuration method.

Routers that join several LISs SHOULD (RECOMMENDED) support a separate set of parameters for each, ideally with one physical interface. The last octet of an NSAPA, the selector, can tell apart up to 256 LISs for the same end system identifier.
sections.eli5: A LIS is like one street where every house has the same street name. To visit another street you must go through the post office, which is the router.

sections.title: Encapsulation and the Default MTU
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support IEEE 802.2 LLC/SNAP encapsulation, which is the default packet format for IP datagrams. Other encapsulations are allowed if agreed in advance or negotiated per virtual connection.

The default IP MTU for AAL5 is 9180 octets, the same as for IP over SMDS in RFC 1209. The RFC explains that large frames help applications such as NFS (which prefers at least 8300 octets), reduce fragmentation, and help routers, whose costs track packets handled more than bytes moved. This text comes from RFC 1626.

PVC-only implementations use 9180 unless both sides agreed on another value. SVC implementations MUST try to negotiate the AAL CPCS-SDU size in the AAL Parameters element of the SETUP message, and the called party answers in CONNECT, either accepting the values or asking for a smaller one. If the CONNECT lacks the element that SETUP carried, the caller clears the call. The forward and backward sizes may differ, and valid values run from 1 to 65535.

All routers that conform MUST implement Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191, clarified by RFC 1435). Hosts SHOULD implement it.
sections.eli5: Packets are sent in big boxes, 9180 units wide by default. If two computers want different box sizes they agree on one when they start talking.

sections.title: How ATMARP Servers and Clients Work
sections.content:
For switched connections the LIS has exactly one ATMARP server in this memo. Servers do not open connections. Clients connect to the server over an LLC/SNAP virtual connection, and the server learns from the source addresses of the requests it receives.

To register, a client MUST connect to the server and send an ATMARP_Request asking for its own IP address. If the reply's source addresses match the target addresses, the client is registered. A client with several IP addresses repeats this for each one. It MUST refresh at least every 15 minutes, and it MUST answer ATMARP and InATMARP requests that arrive on any connection.

For each request the server compares source and target IP addresses. A request where both are the same is a registration. If a different ATM address already holds that IP address on another open connection, the server returns the existing entry, raises a "duplicate IP address detected" condition and does not update the table. Otherwise it creates or updates the entry. A request with different addresses is a lookup, answered with a reply or with an ATMARP_NAK if there is no entry. Lookups from unknown clients also create an entry, which lets old RFC 1577 clients register just by sending requests.

Server entries are valid for 20 minutes and then deleted. Client entries last at most 15 minutes. When an entry ages, an open PVC is revalidated with InATMARP, and an open SVC is revalidated by asking the server. If the server says the host is not found, the SVC should be closed and the entry removed. PVC-only clients use InATMARP and make no other address resolution requests.
sections.eli5: There is one phone book keeper. Everyone tells the keeper their address, checks in regularly so the entry does not expire, and asks the keeper when they want to find someone.

sections.title: ATMARP Packet Format
sections.content:
ATMARP and InATMARP packets keep the ARP fields ar$hrd, ar$pro and ar$op in the same byte positions as ARP, but the rest differs and packets have variable length. ar$hrd is 19 (0x0013) for ATMARP and ar$pro is 0x0800 for IP. The operation codes are 1 (ATMARP_Request), 2 (ATMARP_Reply), 8 (InATMARP_Request), 9 (InATMARP_Reply) and 10 (ATMARP_NAK).

Address lengths are carried in type-and-length (TL) bytes. In a TL byte, bit 7 is 0 for an ATM Forum NSAPA and 1 for E.164, and the low 6 bits give an address length from 0 to 20 octets. A length of zero means a null or unknown address, and no storage is allocated for it. Three address structures are defined: NSAPA only, E.164 only, and E.164 with an NSAPA subaddress. Implementations MUST support all three.

An ATMARP_NAK is a copy of the received request with the operation code changed to 10. A client that receives an unsupported operation code MUST discard it quietly. For IPv4, a null protocol address is sent as length zero, though receivers MUST accept the older form of length 4 with 0.0.0.0.

The packets travel in AAL5 using LLC/SNAP, with the LLC value 0xAA-AA-03, the OUI 0x00-00-00 and the EtherType 0x08-06. The LLC/SNAP header is 8 octets.
sections.eli5: Each question or answer is a form with boxes for names and addresses. Boxes you do not need are simply left out so the form is shorter.

sections.title: Broadcast and Multicast
sections.content:
ATM does not support broadcast addressing, so IP broadcast addresses have no mapping to an ATM broadcast service. Members can still send or receive datagrams with any of the four standard IP broadcast address forms, and MUST process a received IP broadcast or subnet broadcast as if it were addressed to them.

ATM also does not directly support IP multicast, so there is no mapping from IP multicast addresses either. The RFC says current multicast implementations such as MBONE and IP tunneling continue to work over ATM-based LISs in a WAN configuration. Both areas are left to future extensions.
sections.eli5: ATM has no way to shout to everyone at once, so this document does not invent one. It leaves that for later.

sections.title: Security and Open Issues
sections.content:
The RFC admits that not all security issues of IP over ATM are well understood. It expects that authenticated call management, authenticated end-to-end communication and encryption will be needed in globally connected ATM networks, but treats them as out of scope.

It notes known problems with host impersonation through address resolution protocols and says no special security mechanism has been added to ATMARP. In its open issues it calls the lack of ATMARP packet authentication a potentially serious flaw, since corrupt information could be put into the server. Other open issues include automatic configuration of client ATM addresses through DHCP or ILMI. Section 12 requires clients to provide the MIB defined in RFC 2320.
sections.eli5: The phone book keeper does not check who is really calling, so a trickster could write a wrong address in it. The authors say this is a worry.

sections.title: What Changed From Earlier RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 2225 updates RFC 1577 and RFC 1626. The changes include a pointer to the classical MIB for setting variables, a list of ATMARP server addresses instead of a single one, and the MTU section replaced by the RFC 1626 text.

Client registration now starts with the first ATMARP_Request instead of an InATMARP exchange. The memo also clarifies the variable-length packet format, the ARP_NAK format, InATMARP with null IPv4 addresses, and registration and replies for clients that hold more than one IP address in a LIS.
sections.eli5: This list says what was fixed since the older versions: one new list of keepers, a clearer way to sign in and a clearer form.

fields.desc: Hardware type, 19 (0x0013) for ATM Forum address family.

fields.desc: Type and length of source ATM number.

fields.name: ar$sstl
fields.desc: Type and length of source ATM subaddress.

fields.name: ar$op
fields.desc: Operation code: request, reply or NAK.

fields.name: ar$spln
fields.desc: Length of source protocol address, 0 or 4.

fields.name: ar$thtl
fields.desc: Type and length of target ATM number.

fields.name: ar$tstl
fields.desc: Type and length of target ATM subaddress.

fields.name: ar$tpln
fields.desc: Length of target protocol address, 0 or 4.

items.label: ATMARP_Request
items.desc: Asks the server to resolve a target IP address, or registers a client when source and target IP match.

items.label: InATMARP_Request
items.desc: Asks the station at the far end of a connection for its addresses.

items.label: ATMARP_NAK
items.desc: Negative reply: a copy of the request with the code changed.
